title: Turtles All the Way Down
summary:
An old story, told in many versions: a scientist gives a lecture on astronomy, and afterwards an old lady tells him it is all rubbish. The world is a flat plate, she says, resting on the back of a giant tortoise. And what is the tortoise standing on? "It's turtles all the way down!" Stephen Hawking opened A Brief History of Time (1988) with it; William James told a version with rocks in 1882; and John Locke in 1689 used the Indian picture of the world on an elephant on a tortoise to mock explanations that explain nothing.

It is the picture of an infinite regress: every support needs a support. There seem to be only three ways out, sometimes called Agrippa's or Münchhausen's trilemma: the chain goes on forever; it stops at something that holds itself up (a foundation, a first cause, a brute fact); or it loops round, and the parts hold each other up. Each has its defenders, in the theory of knowledge (what justifies what we believe?) and in arguments about why there is anything at all.
citations: Stephen Hawking, A Brief History of Time (Bantam, 1988), ch. 1
William James, "Rationality, Activity and Faith," The Princeton Review (July 1882) ("rocks all the way down")
John Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689), Book II, ch. 23, § 2
Ross Cameron, "Infinite Regress Arguments," Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/infinite-regress/
